### The own checker makes a division or product of equal operands one value: a functional-consistency lemma before any circuit is built

change `lrswmqvktrmy` · [log `f67e8c835e0a`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3761db96-b870-47f7-aded-2ba264c165f4/f67e8c835e0a9e3fd91473191d986f0eef13e83a52620ff2b8a981fb5cf29d11.jsonl.gz)

The own checker leaves divisions and multiplications to the solver as fresh bits under facts, and shares one only when its operand terms are identical. Two operations on equal values written differently (Math.abs(hash) % n and (hash & 0x7fffffff) % n, for a hash that is not negative) were separate unknowns, so the solver answered them differently, each model was refined, both 32-bit dividers were built, and the solver was left proving two dividers equivalent: benchmark case real/bucket/fix-confined ran out of time (over 100 s; 20 s deadline: 2 of 2 divisions built, 53,649 clauses).

Now, when a model gives two operations of one kind and width equal operands (a product's in either order) but different results, bits.rs adds the lemma (a1 == a2 && b1 == b2) -> (q1 == q2 && r1 == r2) and solves again, before refining any operation (Blaster::inconsistent_pair, add_congruence; the engine's solve loop). The lemma holds of every real operation, so it rules out no real execution; for a division by zero, whose bits nothing reads, it only picks equal values.

### Confirming a proof that rests on contracts: under --confirm, JBMC applies the own checker's contracts at the same calls and proves it again

change `knonkrpproky` · [log `261e85d7b862`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3761db96-b870-47f7-aded-2ba264c165f4/261e85d7b8624a58d58746c317c21b709baa77f38ad2e74720230fcb211be8e8.jsonl.gz)

**Reply:**

I measured `fix-confined` with a 20 s deadline and it confirms the theory. Both analyses are below; you said you'd decide from them.

## 1. `real/bucket/fix-confined` runs out of time

**What happens.** The two versions are `Math.abs(hash) % buckets` and `(hash & 0x7fffffff) % buckets`, with `hash < 0` excluded by the scope. The run took 3 paths and 6 solver calls, and **both divisions were built in full (2 of 2)**. Then the solver timed out on about 53,600 clauses.

**Why.** For a non-negative hash, both dividends equal `hash`, but they are different terms. The own checker gives each division fresh quotient and remainder bits, constrained only by general facts about division, and it shares a division only when its operand terms are identical. So nothing says "equal operands give equal results." The solver picks different remainders for equal dividends. Each model is caught as wrong, the division circuit is built, and the solver is left proving two 32-bit dividers equivalent. That is a classically hard problem for a SAT solver.

**The fix.** Add functional consistency (an Ackermann lemma) to the refinement loop in `bmc/bits.rs`:
- When a model gives two divisions, or two multiplications, equal operand values but different results, add the clause (a₁ = a₂ ∧ b₁ = b₂) → (q₁ = q₂ ∧ r₁ = r₂) before building any circuit.
- Here the solver then only has to show `hash & 0x7fffffff == hash` for `hash ≥ 0`, which is trivial. Neither divider would be built.
